claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of high-entropy solid-solution nanoparticles across 473–1923 K is governed by the degree of local chemical ordering.
Increasing local chemical ordering increases the activation barriers for atomic diffusion.
Enhanced d-orbital coupling is responsible for the LCO-induced increase in atomic-diffusion barriers.
Greater local chemical ordering makes the energy landscape more rugged.
LCO-induced diffusion barriers maintain elemental homogeneity and preserve a single-phase solid solution.
Low local chemical ordering permits faster atomic rearrangement.
Faster atomic rearrangement causes phase segregation and structural degradation.
The target materials are nanoparticles containing at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially having a single-phase solid-solution structure.
Cooling rate or pre-annealing can be used to produce different degrees of local chemical ordering at fixed overall composition.
Comparing particles with identical overall composition and different LCO under an identical thermal protocol controls for composition and thermal history.
Using an inert atmosphere is intended to prevent oxidation from confounding the comparison.
Higher-LCO nanoparticles will retain their original single-phase structure after thermal cycling.
Higher-LCO nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous elemental distribution after thermal cycling.
Lower-LCO nanoparticles will show more phase separation or elemental segregation than higher-LCO nanoparticles.
Lower-LCO nanoparticles will show more grain growth than higher-LCO nanoparticles.
The proposed LCO-controlled stability relationship holds under inert conditions throughout 473–1923 K.
Oxidative or other extrinsic environmental effects can alter diffusion behavior and stability.
The quantitative relationship among processing-induced LCO, diffusion activation energy, and phase stability is not established.
